name: Business & Economics
tagline: From everyday choices to organizations, markets and economic research.

nodes.title: Needs, Wants and Choices
nodes.goal: Recognize everyday needs and make a choice when there is not enough for everything.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish a basic need from an optional want.

lesson.overview: People need care, water, food and a safe place to rest. People also want many enjoyable things. A choice happens when we cannot do or have everything at once: one basket may hold only two toys, or playtime may end before every game is finished. Naming what we choose and what we leave for later helps us understand a trade-off. Different people can choose differently without either person being wrong.
lesson.worked_example: A toy basket fits two things. Nia chooses a ball and a book, leaving a drum on the shelf. The drum is something she gives up for this trip; she can still enjoy it later.
lesson.activity: With an adult, choose two of three picture cards to pack for pretend play. Name what stays behind, then try another choice.
lesson.reflection: When might water matter more than a new toy?

quiz.prompt: You are thirsty. What meets that need?
quiz.explain: Water meets the need to drink.
quiz.say: You are thirsty. What meets that need?

quiz.prompt: Your bag fits one toy. You choose a bear. What happens to the drum?
quiz.explain: A limit means one option is left behind.
quiz.say: Your bag fits one toy. You choose a bear. What happens to the drum?

quiz.prompt: Which is usually a want rather than a basic need?
quiz.explain: A balloon can be enjoyable, but people can meet basic needs without it.
quiz.say: Which is usually a want rather than a basic need?

quiz.prompt: A friend chooses a puzzle instead of your game. Can both choices be okay?
quiz.explain: People can enjoy different activities.
quiz.say: A friend chooses a puzzle instead of your game. Can both choices be okay?

quiz.prompt: There is time for one story. What can you do?
quiz.explain: Choosing helps when time is limited.
quiz.say: There is time for one story. What can you do?

quiz.prompt: You pick drawing instead of blocks. What did you give up this time?
quiz.explain: The unchosen activity is what you give up for this choice.
quiz.say: You pick drawing instead of blocks. What did you give up this time?

nodes.kid_text: We need water, food, care and a safe place. We also like toys and games. Sometimes we choose one thing and leave another for later. You can say, “I pick the ball today.”

nodes.title: Work and Helping
nodes.goal: Describe how people combine different tasks to help a community.
learning_outcomes: Name work that produces an object or a service.
Recognize unpaid helping as a contribution.

lesson.overview: Work changes materials or provides a helpful action. A baker makes bread, a driver moves people, and a carer helps someone feel safe. Some work is paid and some is unpaid; both can matter. A team can divide a big job into smaller tasks, but it must also share information. We notice what each person contributes rather than deciding that only the most visible job counts.
lesson.worked_example: For a pretend picnic, one child lays out cups, another carries napkins, and an adult prepares food. The picnic works because the jobs fit together.
lesson.activity: Build a pretend cafe with blocks. Take turns preparing, carrying and tidying. Tell a partner what you need before switching jobs.
lesson.reflection: Who helps your day go well even when you do not see their work?

quiz.prompt: Who makes bread?
quiz.explain: A baker turns ingredients into bread.
quiz.say: Who makes bread?

quiz.prompt: A neighbour helps carry a bag for free. Is that helpful work?
quiz.explain: Useful work can be unpaid.
quiz.say: A neighbour helps carry a bag for free. Is that helpful work?

quiz.prompt: A team sets a table. What helps?
quiz.explain: Communication helps tasks fit together.
quiz.say: A team sets a table. What helps?

quiz.prompt: A driver takes people to school. What does the driver provide?
quiz.explain: Transport is a service: an action that helps someone.
quiz.say: A driver takes people to school. What does the driver provide?

quiz.prompt: Who should get a turn at the pretend shop?
quiz.explain: Taking turns lets everyone learn the jobs.
quiz.say: Who should get a turn at the pretend shop?

quiz.prompt: The cups are ready but the table is dirty. What task is still needed?
quiz.explain: Teams check which useful task remains.
quiz.say: The cups are ready but the table is dirty. What task is still needed?

nodes.kid_text: People do many helpful jobs. Some make things. Some care for people. You can help too: carry a napkin, tell a friend what is needed, and take turns.

nodes.title: Goods, Services and Exchange
nodes.goal: Explain voluntary exchange and the roles of buyers, sellers and money.
learning_outcomes: Describe why barter can be difficult.
Explain money as a medium of exchange.

lesson.overview: A good is an object such as a pencil; a service is an action such as repairing a bicycle. In barter, people exchange directly. Money makes exchanges easier when two people do not each want the other person’s item, because many participants accept the same medium of exchange. A fair classroom exchange needs clear information and a genuine choice to say no. A price tells us what a seller asks, not whether every person values the item equally.
lesson.worked_example: Ada offers a bookmark for Ben’s marble. Ben does not want the bookmark, so barter stops. In a pretend market using tokens, Ada can sell her bookmark to Cara and use tokens to buy a marble from Ben.
lesson.activity: Run a paper-token market for drawings. Label goods and prices, permit everyone to decline, and explain one exchange that did not happen.
lesson.reflection: Why might two people disagree about whether an exchange is worthwhile?

quiz.prompt: Which purchase is a service?
quiz.explain: Repairing is an action; a pencil and apple are goods.
quiz.say: Which purchase is a service?

quiz.prompt: In barter, Mia offers a shell that Jo does not want. Must Jo trade?
quiz.explain: Voluntary exchange allows either person to decline.
quiz.say: In barter, Mia offers a shell that Jo does not want. Must Jo trade?

quiz.prompt: Why can tokens help a pretend market?
quiz.explain: A shared medium helps people exchange with different trading partners.
quiz.say: Why can tokens help a pretend market?

quiz.prompt: A seller asks four tokens. What is four tokens?
quiz.explain: A price is the amount requested in exchange.
quiz.say: A seller asks four tokens. What is four tokens?

quiz.prompt: Which statement gives a buyer useful information?
choices: The toy has a missing wheel
quiz.answer: The toy has a missing wheel
quiz.explain: Clear information helps people decide.
quiz.say: Which statement gives a buyer useful information?

quiz.prompt: One child loves puzzles and another loves balls. What follows?
choices: They may value the same item differently
quiz.answer: They may value the same item differently
quiz.explain: Preferences can differ between people.
quiz.say: One child loves puzzles and another loves balls. What follows?

nodes.kid_text: A good is a thing, like a book. A service is help, like fixing a bike. People may swap things if both agree. Money is something many people accept when they buy and sell.

nodes.title: Resources and a Small Enterprise
nodes.goal: Plan a small pretend enterprise using limited materials, costs and teamwork.
learning_outcomes: List inputs needed for a product.
Compute simple revenue and recorded cost.
Explain a limitation of a classroom profit model.

lesson.overview: An enterprise organizes people and resources to provide something others value. Materials, time, tools and skills all constrain what can be made. Revenue is the amount received from sales; costs are the resources used, expressed in money in a simple account. Revenue minus recorded costs gives a simple profit or loss. This classroom calculation is a model, so we must say whether donated materials or time have been left out.
lesson.worked_example: A class uses six paper sheets costing one token each to make six cards. Selling all six at two tokens brings twelve tokens. Recorded paper cost is six, leaving six tokens before any other costs.
lesson.activity: Plan a pretend card stall with a fixed number of sheets. List inputs, assign jobs, calculate possible revenue and say which costs your model leaves out.
lesson.reflection: How could a project earn tokens while still wasting time or materials?

quiz.prompt: Five cards sell for two tokens each. Revenue is?
quiz.explain: Revenue is quantity sold times price: 5 × 2 = 10.
quiz.say: Five cards sell for two tokens each. Revenue is?

quiz.prompt: Revenue is ten and recorded costs are six. The difference is?
quiz.explain: Subtract costs from revenue: 10 − 6 = 4.
quiz.say: Revenue is ten and recorded costs are six. The difference is?

quiz.prompt: Which is an input for paper cards?
quiz.explain: Paper is used to produce the cards.
quiz.say: Which is an input for paper cards?

quiz.prompt: Only three sheets remain and each card needs one. How many cards can be made now?
quiz.explain: The available material limits production.
quiz.say: Only three sheets remain and each card needs one. How many cards can be made now?

quiz.prompt: An adult donated glue. What should the class say?
quiz.explain: A transparent account identifies donated resources.
quiz.say: An adult donated glue. What should the class say?

quiz.prompt: Customers want stronger cards. What is a useful response?
quiz.explain: Feedback can guide a test of product quality.
quiz.say: Customers want stronger cards. What is a useful response?

nodes.kid_text: A little shop needs materials, time and helpers. Count what comes in and what gets used. You can test an idea, listen to people, and improve it.

nodes.title: Supply, Demand and Market Signals
nodes.goal: Use a simple market table to explain shortages, surpluses and price responses.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish a price change from a shift in demand.

lesson.overview: A demand schedule records how much buyers would purchase at different prices, holding other influences fixed. A supply schedule records how much sellers would offer. If planned purchases exceed planned sales, there is a shortage at that price; the reverse is a surplus. In a competitive model, price adjustments can move plans toward agreement. Real markets also depend on information, rules, market power and access, so equilibrium is a prediction under assumptions rather than a guarantee of fairness.
lesson.worked_example: At a price of two tokens, buyers want eight bookmarks but sellers offer four: a shortage of four. At four tokens, buyers want five and sellers offer five. These schedules meet at five bookmarks and four tokens.
lesson.activity: Plot two supplied schedules. Mark a shortage, a surplus and their intersection. Change buyers’ interest and distinguish that demand shift from moving along the original curve.
lesson.reflection: Why does a market-clearing outcome not tell us whether everyone has what they need?

quiz.prompt: Buyers want nine apples and sellers offer six at one price. The shortage is?
quiz.explain: Planned purchases exceed supply by 9 − 6 = 3.

quiz.prompt: Sellers offer ten loaves while buyers want seven. What exists?
quiz.explain: Supply exceeds demand by three loaves.

quiz.prompt: On a fixed demand curve, a lower price commonly means?
quiz.explain: The model holds other factors fixed and varies quantity with price.

quiz.prompt: A popular game makes more people want its cards at every price. This is?
quiz.explain: Interest changes the whole schedule.

quiz.prompt: Where schedules show equal quantities, the model has?
quiz.explain: Equilibrium means planned purchases and sales agree.

quiz.prompt: Why might a market outcome still be unfair?
quiz.explain: Clearing a market does not guarantee access or a desired distribution.

quiz.prompt: At five tokens, supply is twelve and demand is eight. How many items remain unsold in this plan?
quiz.explain: The planned surplus is 12 − 8 = 4.

quiz.prompt: A storm destroys part of a crop. Holding demand fixed, which change fits the model?
quiz.explain: Less crop is available at each price.

quiz.prompt: A price ceiling below the model’s equilibrium price may produce?
quiz.explain: At a below-equilibrium price, demand can exceed supply.

quiz.prompt: Two markets have the same equilibrium quantity. Must their prices match?
quiz.explain: Different supply and demand schedules can intersect at different prices.

quiz.prompt: At three tokens, buyers plan to buy twelve notebooks and sellers offer eight. Explain the gap and the pressure predicted by a simple competitive model.
quiz.answer: There is a shortage of four notebooks. With demand exceeding supply at that price, the model predicts upward pressure on price, holding other influences fixed.
quiz.explain: There is a shortage of four notebooks. With demand exceeding supply at that price, the model predicts upward pressure on price, holding other influences fixed.

nodes.title: Public Goods and Spillovers
nodes.goal: Identify effects on bystanders and compare ways communities provide shared benefits.
learning_outcomes: Apply rivalry and exclusion tests separately.

lesson.overview: An externality is a benefit or cost affecting people outside an exchange. A noisy workshop may disturb neighbours even when its customers are satisfied. A public good in the economic sense is difficult to exclude people from and does not become substantially less available when another person uses it. These are two separate tests; a resource such as a crowded fishery can be hard to exclude people from yet rival in use. Communities use rules, cooperation and public provision to address problems, each with practical trade-offs.
lesson.worked_example: A lighthouse beam helps another nearby ship without using up the beam, and excluding a ship is difficult. Fish in an open lake differ: a fish caught by one person cannot be caught by another.
lesson.activity: Sort fictional examples by whether users can be excluded and whether one person’s use leaves less for others. For a noisy workshop, suggest one remedy and one possible drawback.
lesson.reflection: Who should be included when a decision affects people outside the buying and selling group?

quiz.prompt: A factory’s noise disturbs nearby residents. This is?
quiz.explain: The cost reaches people outside the sale.

quiz.prompt: One person catches a fish, leaving fewer for others. Fish are?
quiz.explain: One person’s use removes a fish from others’ use.

quiz.prompt: A pure public good has which pair?
quiz.explain: Public-good classification depends on use and exclusion, not who owns it.

quiz.prompt: A garden attracts pollinators to neighbouring gardens. This may be?
quiz.explain: Neighbours may receive benefits without taking part in the original decision.

quiz.prompt: Why can voluntary funding of a shared beacon be difficult?
choices: Benefits used up by each ship
quiz.explain: A free-rider problem can arise when contributors cannot exclude others.

quiz.prompt: Which question improves a noise rule?
quiz.explain: Good analysis considers affected groups and likely consequences.

quiz.prompt: A crowded road is difficult to exclude users from, but extra cars slow others. Which feature is present?
quiz.explain: Congestion means one user affects availability or quality for others.

quiz.prompt: A workshop installs sound insulation. The most direct spillover change is?
quiz.explain: Insulation reduces the external noise reaching nearby people.

quiz.prompt: A rule limits fishing but nobody monitors catches. Which issue should be checked?
quiz.explain: Enforcement and cooperation affect actual resource use.

quiz.prompt: A shared garden plan benefits residents but blocks a delivery path. What should analysis include?
quiz.explain: The plan affects different uses of the shared space.

quiz.prompt: A busy open-access lake is losing fish. Explain why it differs from a non-rival public good and suggest one issue a management plan should address.
quiz.answer: Fish are rival because a catch leaves fewer for others. Access is difficult to exclude, so a management plan should address shared use, monitoring and cooperation.
quiz.explain: Fish are rival because a catch leaves fewer for others. Access is difficult to exclude, so a management plan should address shared use, monitoring and cooperation.

nodes.title: Accounts, Operations and Enterprise Decisions
nodes.goal: Interpret simplified accounts and compare capacity, cash and profitability.

lesson.overview: An income statement summarizes revenues and expenses over a period, while a balance sheet describes assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. Cash flow follows actual receipts and payments; a profitable operation can still face a cash shortage when customers pay later. Operations analysis adds physical constraints: a slow step can limit an entire process. Useful enterprise decisions connect these representations, state assumptions, and compare alternatives rather than treating a single profit number as the whole story.
lesson.worked_example: A studio records revenue of 1,000 units and expenses of 700, giving profit of 300. Customers have paid only 400 so far while 600 has been paid out. Net cash movement is −200 despite the recorded profit.
lesson.activity: Create simplified profit and cash summaries for a fictional workshop. Map three production steps and find the bottleneck. Explain why buying a faster non-bottleneck machine may not increase output.
lesson.reflection: Which missing cost or timing detail could reverse your recommendation?

quiz.prompt: Assets are 900 and liabilities are 350. Equity is?
quiz.explain: The accounting identity gives equity = 900 − 350 = 550.

quiz.prompt: A sale is recorded but the customer has not paid. What can differ?
quiz.explain: Under accrual accounting recognition and payment can occur in different periods.

quiz.prompt: Steps can process 8, 5 and 9 items per hour. Maximum steady flow is?
quiz.explain: The five-item step is the bottleneck under this simple model.

quiz.prompt: A balance sheet describes?
quiz.explain: It is a snapshot, unlike a period-based income statement.

quiz.prompt: Revenue is 200 and expenses 240. Result?
quiz.explain: Expenses exceed revenue by 40.

quiz.prompt: A faster machine replaces a non-bottleneck step. Output may not rise because?
quiz.explain: Capacity elsewhere cannot remove the remaining bottleneck.

quiz.prompt: A workshop buys equipment with borrowed cash. Immediately, the simplified balance sheet adds?
quiz.explain: Equipment is an asset and the borrowing creates an obligation.

quiz.prompt: Cash starts at 100, receipts are 80 and payments are 130. Closing cash is?
quiz.explain: Closing cash is 100 + 80 − 130 = 50.

quiz.prompt: A process bottleneck rises from five to seven units per hour; other steps handle eight and nine. New capacity is?
quiz.explain: The improved seven-unit step is still the slowest.

quiz.prompt: Two firms report the same profit but different payment delays. Which measure may differ?
quiz.explain: Timing of collection can produce different cash positions.

quiz.prompt: A studio records a profitable sale this month, but payment arrives next month and wages are due now. Explain why profit does not settle its immediate problem.
quiz.answer: Recorded revenue can exceed expenses while cash receipts arrive later. The studio must consider payment timing because profit is different from cash available for wages.
quiz.explain: Recorded revenue can exceed expenses while cash receipts arrive later. The studio must consider payment timing because profit is different from cash available for wages.

nodes.title: Economic Indicators and Policy Trade-offs
nodes.goal: Interpret inflation, output and unemployment without confusing indicators with wellbeing.

lesson.overview: Gross domestic product measures the value of final production within an economy over a period. Nominal changes mix price and quantity changes; real measures adjust for price change using a stated method. Inflation is a rate of change of a price index, so lower inflation does not necessarily mean falling prices. Unemployment statistics depend on definitions of employment, job search and the population counted. Policy arguments combine these imperfect measurements with models, uncertainty and value judgements about whose outcomes matter.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional price index rises from 100 to 110 and then to 115.5. Inflation falls from 10% to 5%, although the price level rises both years. Describing the second year as falling prices would confuse a rate with a level.
lesson.activity: Calculate nominal growth and a simple price-adjusted growth estimate from a fictional dataset. Add one wellbeing measure not captured well by GDP and explain its relevance.
lesson.reflection: Could production rise while some people become worse off? Explain a mechanism.

quiz.prompt: An index rises from 100 to 105. Inflation is?
quiz.explain: The percentage change is (105 − 100) / 100 = 5%.

quiz.prompt: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%. Prices usually?
quiz.explain: Positive inflation means the price level still increases.

quiz.prompt: Nominal output rises only because prices rise. Real output is?
quiz.explain: Price adjustment removes the price-only increase.

quiz.prompt: Why count final goods rather than every intermediate sale in GDP?
quiz.explain: The value of intermediate inputs is already embodied in final production.

quiz.prompt: GDP per person rises. What is not guaranteed?
quiz.explain: An average can conceal unequal changes across people.

quiz.prompt: A policy debate compares job gains and environmental damage. It requires?
quiz.explain: Measurement informs choices but does not remove trade-offs.

quiz.prompt: A price index falls from 120 to 114. The rate of change is?
quiz.explain: The change −6 divided by 120 is −5%.

quiz.prompt: Nominal output rises 10% and the price index rises 10%. Simplified real growth is?
quiz.explain: The quantity ratio is 1.10 / 1.10 = 1.

quiz.prompt: A report compares unemployment across places using different definitions. First check?
choices: The colours used in the report
quiz.explain: Consistent definitions are needed for meaningful comparison.

quiz.prompt: GDP rises after expensive pollution cleanup. Why is wellbeing ambiguous?
quiz.explain: Measured production does not directly subtract every environmental harm.

quiz.prompt: Inflation falls from 9% to 4%. A headline says “Prices are falling.” Explain the mistake.
quiz.answer: Inflation is a rate of change in the price level. A positive rate of four percent means prices still rise, but more slowly; falling inflation is not necessarily a falling price level.
quiz.explain: Inflation is a rate of change in the price level. A positive rate of four percent means prices still rise, but more slowly; falling inflation is not necessarily a falling price level.

nodes.title: Microeconomic Models and Strategic Behaviour
nodes.goal: Analyze constrained choice, marginal reasoning and strategic interaction.
learning_outcomes: Apply marginal reasoning to a constrained choice.
Identify best responses and Nash equilibrium.
Critique the welfare implications of an equilibrium.

lesson.overview: Microeconomic models describe choices under constraints and make their assumptions explicit. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit of an action with its additional cost; sunk costs are already incurred and cannot be changed by the current decision. Strategic interaction arises when an action’s payoff depends on others’ choices. A Nash equilibrium is a profile in which no player gains from a unilateral deviation, given the others’ actions. Equilibrium need not maximize collective welfare, and a model’s predictive value must be tested against institutions, information and observed behaviour.
lesson.worked_example: Two firms choose Clean or Pollute. Clean/Clean gives each 3; Pollute against Clean gives 4 to the polluter and 0 to the cleaner; Pollute/Pollute gives each 1. Each prefers Pollute whatever the other does, so that equilibrium yields less combined payoff than Clean/Clean.
lesson.activity: Construct a two-player payoff table, identify each best response, and test a rule change. Explain which assumptions about monitoring and incentives make the changed prediction plausible.
lesson.reflection: When might a predicted equilibrium fail because participants understand the game differently?

quiz.prompt: An unrecoverable past expense is?
quiz.explain: Current alternatives cannot change a sunk cost.

quiz.prompt: An extra unit benefits a firm by 7 and costs 5. Its net marginal benefit is?
quiz.explain: The incremental gain is 7 − 5 = 2.

quiz.prompt: A Nash equilibrium requires?
choices: An equal payoff for each player
quiz.explain: Each action is a best response to the others at that profile.

quiz.prompt: A dominant strategy is optimal?
quiz.explain: Dominance compares an action across all opposing choices.

quiz.prompt: Changing an enforcement rule may change behaviour by?
quiz.explain: Institutions shape incentives and feasible choices.

quiz.prompt: A model predicts poorly in a new setting. Best response?
quiz.explain: Models require empirical evaluation and may have limited scope.

quiz.prompt: A firm can earn 20 by staying put or 24 by deviating while rivals stay put. Is the current profile Nash?
quiz.explain: A player can improve by changing its own action.

quiz.prompt: An extra service slot earns 30 but uses labour worth 35. The marginal comparison favours?
choices: Add the slot at that cost
quiz.explain: Its incremental cost exceeds its incremental benefit.

quiz.prompt: A repeated interaction makes future cooperation valuable. Which assumption in a one-shot game changes?
choices: The value of past sunk costs
quiz.explain: Future consequences can alter incentives today.

quiz.prompt: Two equilibria exist in a coordination game. What remains to explain?
quiz.explain: Equilibrium multiplicity leaves a selection question.

quiz.prompt: Two firms are at a proposed equilibrium, but one can raise its payoff by changing its action while the other stays put. Explain what this reveals.
quiz.answer: The profile is not a Nash equilibrium because a profitable unilateral deviation exists. The changing firm’s action was not a best response to the other firm.
quiz.explain: The profile is not a Nash equilibrium because a profitable unilateral deviation exists. The changing firm’s action was not a best response to the other firm.

nodes.title: Business Evidence and Causal Questions
nodes.goal: Distinguish causal effects from associations and design a transparent evaluation.
learning_outcomes: Specify an evaluation with a primary outcome.

lesson.overview: A business or economic claim becomes a causal question when it asks what would change under an intervention. The counterfactual outcome for the same unit under the alternative intervention is unobserved, so comparison design matters. Random assignment can create comparable groups in expectation, but attrition, spillovers and noncompliance complicate analysis. Regression can summarize conditional associations without automatically removing confounding. A credible report specifies the population, intervention, outcome, uncertainty, costs and ethical constraints before interpreting a result.
lesson.worked_example: Customers who choose a training course earn more later. This association may reflect prior motivation. Randomly offering eligible volunteers access creates a clearer comparison of the offer’s effect, although the result applies to that offer and study population.
lesson.activity: Design a fictional evaluation of a new ordering system. Specify assignment, primary outcome, follow-up period and a possible spillover. Write a short pre-analysis plan without collecting real customer data.
lesson.reflection: What difference between your study participants and a new business could limit transfer?

quiz.prompt: Higher sales among shops choosing training establish?
quiz.explain: Pre-existing differences may explain the association.

quiz.prompt: Random assignment balances groups?
quiz.explain: Randomization supports comparability probabilistically, not perfect realized equality.

quiz.prompt: One trained worker teaches untreated colleagues. This is?
quiz.explain: The intervention can affect comparison units through interaction.

quiz.prompt: A primary outcome should ideally be chosen?
quiz.explain: Advance specification reduces selective reporting.

quiz.prompt: A narrow confidence interval mainly indicates?
quiz.explain: Precision does not establish validity or generalizability.

quiz.prompt: Participants leave one study arm more often. Concern?
quiz.explain: Unequal missingness can undermine comparable observed groups.

quiz.prompt: A treatment group improves by 5, but no comparison is observed. What is unresolved?
quiz.explain: The counterfactual may also have improved.

quiz.prompt: Random assignment occurs by store. What uncertainty structure is relevant?
quiz.explain: Shared assignment and conditions create clustering.

quiz.prompt: A study measures twelve outcomes and reports one positive result. Request?
choices: The full outcome plan and results
quiz.answer: The full outcome plan and results
quiz.explain: Selective reporting can exaggerate evidence.

quiz.prompt: A pilot works in highly trained branches. Transfer to other branches requires?
quiz.explain: Capacity and context can change effects.

quiz.prompt: Shops that volunteer for coaching later sell more. Propose a clearer evaluation and name a limit it would retain.
quiz.answer: Random assignment of coaching offers among eligible shops would reduce selection differences. A comparison estimates the offer effect, but spillovers and generalization beyond the sample still need attention.
quiz.explain: Random assignment of coaching offers among eligible shops would reduce selection differences. A comparison estimates the offer effect, but spillovers and generalization beyond the sample still need attention.

nodes.title: Applied Econometrics and Identification
nodes.goal: Build and critique a causal identification strategy for an economic policy question.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate identification assumptions separately from statistical precision.
Design robustness analyses and state their limits.

lesson.overview: Applied econometrics begins with a clearly defined estimand and a justification for how observed comparisons recover it. In a two-group, two-period difference-in-differences design, the treated group’s change is compared with the untreated group’s change. A causal interpretation requires that their untreated potential outcomes would have followed parallel trends, alongside conditions such as no anticipation and an appropriate treatment definition. Pre-treatment patterns can reveal problems but cannot prove the unobserved post-treatment counterfactual. Researchers examine sensitivity, spillovers, composition changes and the dependence structure that informs uncertainty.
lesson.worked_example: A treated region’s mean outcome rises from 40 to 52, while a comparison region rises from 30 to 35. Difference-in-differences is (52 − 40) − (35 − 30) = 7. A simultaneous reform only in the treated region would challenge attributing all seven units to the policy of interest.
lesson.activity: Write a research proposal using a fictional regional panel. Define the estimand, draw a causal diagram, justify the comparison, state identification assumptions, and plan placebo and sensitivity analyses. Critique what those checks cannot establish.
lesson.reflection: Which untestable assumption carries the largest burden in your design, and what substantive evidence supports it?

quiz.prompt: Treated outcomes rise 12 and comparison outcomes rise 5. DiD is?
quiz.explain: Subtract the comparison change from the treated change.

quiz.prompt: Parallel trends concerns?
quiz.explain: Groups can start at different levels while having equal counterfactual changes.

quiz.prompt: An insignificant pre-trend test proves parallel trends?
quiz.explain: Failure to reject may reflect low power and cannot establish the post-treatment counterfactual.

quiz.prompt: A treatment-specific concurrent reform threatens?
quiz.explain: The additional reform can produce a different untreated trajectory or compound treatment.

quiz.prompt: Why consider clustering uncertainty by region?
quiz.explain: Standard errors should reflect the relevant dependence and assignment structure.

quiz.prompt: A sensitivity analysis is most useful when it?
quiz.explain: Sensitivity quantifies how much the conclusion depends on uncertain assumptions.

quiz.prompt: A policy is announced before implementation and behaviour changes early. Which design issue arises?
quiz.explain: Pre-treatment periods may already be affected.

quiz.prompt: Treatment regions lose low-income residents after a reform. Mean income rises. Examine?
quiz.explain: Population changes can produce apparent effects unrelated to individual gains.

quiz.prompt: A neighbouring untreated region benefits from the policy. The comparison may be?
quiz.explain: The control outcome is affected by treatment elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: An estimate is precise but rests on implausible parallel trends. The priority is?
quiz.explain: Statistical precision cannot repair an invalid comparison.

quiz.prompt: A DiD estimate is positive and pre-trend tests are insignificant, but a second reform began only in treated regions. Critique the causal claim.
quiz.answer: An insignificant pre-trend test cannot prove parallel trends in the counterfactual period. The concurrent reform is a rival cause, so attribution to the target policy needs substantive evidence and sensitivity analysis.
quiz.explain: An insignificant pre-trend test cannot prove parallel trends in the counterfactual period. The concurrent reform is a rival cause, so attribution to the target policy needs substantive evidence and sensitivity analysis.

nodes.title: Strategy, Organizations and Research Synthesis
nodes.goal: Develop a research-based organizational recommendation with competing explanations and an evaluation plan.
learning_outcomes: Synthesize evidence into a falsifiable pilot recommendation.

lesson.overview: Strategy research examines how organizations allocate capabilities under competition, uncertainty and institutional constraints. A useful explanation connects a mechanism to observable predictions and considers rival explanations such as selection, timing or market conditions. Case evidence can illuminate processes without establishing how common they are; quantitative evidence can estimate patterns while missing local context. Research synthesis assesses design quality, relevance and heterogeneity before recommending action. A defensible recommendation names whose outcomes count, a reversible pilot where feasible, stopping criteria and the evidence that would change the decision.
lesson.worked_example: Three successful firms use flexible teams, but failed firms were never sampled. The cases suggest a coordination mechanism, yet survivorship bias prevents concluding that flexible teams cause success. A better study adds unsuccessful cases and tests a phased pilot with predetermined coordination and service measures.
lesson.activity: Prepare a master’s-level strategy brief for a fictional cooperative. Compare two theories, build an evidence table with validity concerns, propose a pilot and measurement plan, and write a rival explanation for the expected result.
lesson.reflection: What result would make you abandon your preferred organizational explanation?

quiz.prompt: Studying only firms that survived risks?
quiz.explain: Excluded failures can change the apparent relation between strategy and success.

quiz.prompt: A mechanism describes?
choices: A list of firms without a claim
A process linking action to outcome
quiz.answer: A process linking action to outcome
quiz.explain: Mechanisms connect actions to intermediate processes and outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A convincing strategy brief should include?
quiz.explain: Falsifiable claims permit learning and revision.

quiz.prompt: Conflicting study results may reflect?
choices: A need to discard mixed findings
A need to average without appraisal
quiz.explain: Heterogeneity requires explanation rather than automatic dismissal.

quiz.prompt: A pilot stopping rule should be specified?
quiz.explain: Advance criteria make evaluation and decisions more transparent.

quiz.prompt: A rich case study most directly supports?
quiz.explain: Case depth can reveal mechanisms while leaving prevalence and generalization uncertain.

quiz.prompt: A firm credits a new structure for growth during an industry boom. A rival explanation is?
choices: The wording of the mission title
quiz.explain: External demand may explain growth independently of the reorganization.

quiz.prompt: A theory predicts quicker decisions through fewer approval steps. Useful mechanism evidence is?
quiz.explain: The proposed process concerns decision latency.

quiz.prompt: A synthesis finds gains in stable markets and losses in volatile ones. The recommendation should?
quiz.explain: The pattern suggests effect heterogeneity relevant to strategy.

quiz.prompt: A pilot improves speed but increases employee turnover. Next analysis should?
quiz.explain: Organizational recommendations need multiple consequences and causal scrutiny.

quiz.prompt: A strategy paper studies successful firms using flexible teams and recommends universal adoption. Identify a research weakness and a better next study.
quiz.answer: Sampling successful firms creates survivorship bias and hides failures. Compare relevant unsuccessful cases and test the proposed coordination mechanism in a bounded pilot with explicit outcomes.
quiz.explain: Sampling successful firms creates survivorship bias and hides failures. Compare relevant unsuccessful cases and test the proposed coordination mechanism in a bounded pilot with explicit outcomes.
